parts.title: Reporting a heating problem
parts.context: A tenant phones a letting agency about a broken boiler.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a tenant phoning a letting agency to report a problem in her flat. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Castle Lettings, Neil speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: Hello. I'm a tenant in one of your flats, and I need to report a problem with the heating. It's in the kitchen, and it's getting worse.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The problem is in the kitchen, so 'kitchen' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: Aisha Rahman. That's R-A-H-M-A-N.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Thank you, Ms Rahman. And which flat are you in?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: Flat nine, Kingsley House. It's on the third floor.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: What exactly is the problem?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: The boiler is making a loud banging noise, and it isn't heating the water properly. I've had no hot water since the morning.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: How long has it been going on?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: The noise started three days ago, but it only stopped working this morning.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Have you contacted anyone already?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: I rang the emergency number on the notice in the hall, but I only got an answerphone, and nobody has called me back.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: I'm sorry about that. The landlord, Mr Walsh, has been informed, and I'll arrange for an engineer to visit. I can't offer you today, but I can offer you tomorrow. Friday is also possible, but I assume you'd rather not wait.

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: No, tomorrow would be much better. What time will the engineer come?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Between eleven and one. The engineer will phone you about half an hour before arriving.

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: I'm working from home tomorrow, so that's fine. Do I need to do anything?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Please make sure that somebody is at home, because the engineer must get into the flat and the boiler cupboard. Could you also clear the space around the boiler?

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: Of course. And what about tonight? It's quite cold.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: We'll lend you an electric heater. The caretaker, Mr Dunn, lives on the ground floor, and he can bring one up this afternoon.

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: That's very kind. How will I know the appointment is confirmed?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: I'll send you a confirmation by email within the next hour, with the details.

script.speaker: aisha
script.text: Thank you very much for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A residents' meeting
parts.context: A council officer explains improvements to a housing estate.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a council officer talking to residents about improvements to a housing estate. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Raj Banerjee, from the housing department, and I'm here to tell you about the improvements planned for the Elm Estate.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: First, the money. Some residents have asked whether your rents will go up to pay for this, and I can promise you that they won't. The money comes from a lottery grant, which the council applied for last year, and we were delighted when it was approved.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: The total is two hundred thousand pounds. It's not as much as some people hoped, so we've had to decide what comes first, and you told us in the survey that safety was the priority. So the first thing to be built will be the new lighting, along all the footpaths.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: The play area is being moved. Many parents told us that the old one was out of sight, so they couldn't watch their children from their windows. The new one will be right in front of the main block, close to the flats.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: There will also be a community garden, where residents can grow vegetables and herbs. The council will provide the soil, the tools and some training, and the produce will belong to whoever grows it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: Building work will start in June, as soon as the school term finishes, so that the noise doesn't disturb the children who are revising. It should be finished by the end of September.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: There are some changes you should know about. Parking permits will be introduced, because at present people who don't live here leave their cars on the estate. Each household will get one free permit, and a second will cost a small fee.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: From the first of next month, bins will be collected on Thursdays, not Mondays. The change is to fit in with the new rounds in the rest of the area, and there will be reminders on the notice boards.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: We know that not everybody can come to meetings, so there will be drop-in sessions in the community hall every Saturday morning in May, where you can look at the plans and talk to the team.

script.speaker: banerjee
script.text: To end tonight, we'd like you to vote on the design of the play area. There are three designs on the tables at the back. Please take a ballot paper, and the votes will be counted while we all have a cup of tea. Thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Preparing for a mock trial
parts.context: Two law students plan their defence in a mock trial.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two law students, Zoe and Kareem, preparing for a mock trial. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: Kareem, have you read the case file for the mock trial? We have to decide our strategy by Thursday.

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: Yes. We're the defence, which is harder, because the evidence against our client looks strong.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: Remind me what the case is. A bicycle shop was broken into, wasn't it?

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: Yes, a bicycle shop was burgled at night, and our client was seen in the street nearby. He says he was walking home from his sister's house.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: That's checkable. His sister can confirm the time he left.

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: What will the judge want from us first?

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: An opening statement, which should be short. Two minutes at most, or the jury will lose interest.

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: Who'll speak?

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: I'll do the opening, and you can do the cross-examination, because you're better at asking questions without getting angry.

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: Thanks, I think. One risk is that our client may not be a good witness. He gets very nervous.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: Then we'll practise with him on Monday. Dr Walsh said the role-play will be recorded, so that we get feedback.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: Let's go through the evidence one piece at a time. The neighbour's statement first.

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: She says she saw him at ten, but she wears glasses, and it was dark, so I'd say it's unreliable.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: The CCTV footage?

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: It's blurred, and you can't see the face, but it supports the defence, because the person on it is much taller than our client.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: The police report?

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: It was written three days later, which is far too late, so we can challenge many of the details.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: The expert witness on fingerprints?

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: She'll use a lot of technical language, and the jury won't understand it, so we must ask her to explain in simple terms.

script.speaker: zoe
script.text: And the shop owner's statement?

script.speaker: kareem
script.text: He gives a different time from the neighbour's, so they contradict each other, and that is our best point. Shall we write it up?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Great Fire of London
parts.context: A history lecture on the fire of 1666.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the Great Fire of London. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. In September sixteen sixty-six, a fire destroyed most of the old city of London. It is one of the best-known disasters in English history, and it started in a very ordinary place: a bakery in Pudding Lane.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why did it spread so quickly? The houses were built mostly of timber, and covered with tar to keep out the rain, and they were packed closely together, with the upper floors leaning towards each other across the narrow streets. The summer had been very dry, and on that Sunday night there was a strong wind blowing from the east, which carried burning pieces from house to house.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The fire burned for four days. By the time it was under control, about thirteen thousand houses and eighty-seven churches had been destroyed, including the old St Paul's Cathedral, and most of the city's people had lost their homes.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Surprisingly, the official number of deaths was very low, only a handful were recorded, although historians suspect that the poor were simply not counted.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The fighting of the fire was chaotic. The most effective method was to demolish houses ahead of the flames, to make gaps that the fire could not cross, and sometimes gunpowder was used to blow the buildings up. But at first the Lord Mayor hesitated, because he didn't want to destroy people's property.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: We know so much about the fire largely thanks to Samuel Pepys, who kept a famous diary. He watched the fire from a boat on the river, as the best way to get a view, and wrote vivid descriptions of what he saw.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: After the fire, the city was rebuilt. The architect Christopher Wren designed a new cathedral, which is the St Paul's we see today, and new houses were required to be made of brick or stone, with wider streets. And a tall column, called the Monument, was built close to the spot where the fire started, as a memorial. Next week we'll look at the Plague.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
